title: Sinking Funds: Never Be 'Surprised' by an Expense Again

lines.say: Christmas is not an emergency.
It happens on December twenty-fifth. Every single year.

scene.text: Most "surprise" expenses run on a schedule.

lines.say: And most of the expenses that wreck a budget work the same way. They're not surprises. They're just not monthly.
The fix is called a sinking fund. Here's exactly how it works, with real numbers.
First, the problem.
Remember the example from episode one? Here's when each cost actually lands.
Annual subscriptions, a hundred and twenty, in January.

lines.cap: Medical copays, $300, spread through the year.
lines.say: Medical copays, three hundred, spread through the year.
Registration, one eighty, in April.

lines.cap: Car repairs, $500, whenever the car decides.
lines.say: Car repairs, five hundred, whenever the car decides.
And the holidays, six hundred, in December.

lines.cap: On a calendar it looks like this. Some months, nothing. Then July brings a $500 repair, and December wants $600.
lines.say: On a calendar, it looks like this. Some months, nothing. Then July brings a five hundred dollar repair, and December wants six hundred.

lines.cap: But averaged out, it's about $142 a month. Or $66 a paycheck.
lines.say: But averaged out, it's about a hundred and forty-two dollars a month. Or sixty-six dollars a paycheck.
Now, here's why paying before beats paying after, even with the exact same money.

items.t: Costs land on a 24% credit card
Then you pay $66 a paycheck toward it

lines.cap: Option one: let the costs land on a credit card at 24%, then pay $66 a paycheck toward it afterward.
lines.say: Option one. Let the costs land on a credit card at twenty-four percent, then pay sixty-six dollars a paycheck toward it afterward.

scene.label: Option one, five years later
scene.sub: still owed, even after paying $66 every single paycheck

lines.cap: Interest builds while you catch up, so you slowly fall behind. After five years you owe $784, and the interest grows every year.
lines.say: Because interest builds while you catch up, you slowly fall behind. After five years, you owe seven hundred and eighty-four dollars, and the interest grows every year.

scene.label: Option two: save the $66 first
scene.sub: owed. The money is waiting when the bill shows up.

lines.cap: Option two: move the same $66 into savings first. When the bill shows up, the money's already there. You owe nothing.
lines.say: Option two. Move the same sixty-six dollars into savings first. When the bill shows up, the money's already there. You owe nothing.
Same money. Opposite results.
So here's how to set them up, in three steps.

scene.text: Your bank statements already know your surprises.

lines.say: Step one. Look backwards. Open last year's bank and card statements, and write down every cost that wasn't monthly.
Holidays, birthdays, car stuff, annual renewals, school costs, the vet. If it happened last year, it'll probably happen again.
Step two. Split them into two kinds. Deadline funds have a date, like car registration, due in April.

lines.cap: Starting in January, that's 7 paychecks away. $180 divided by 7 is $26 a paycheck.
lines.say: Starting in January, that's seven paychecks away. So one eighty, divided by seven, is twenty-six dollars a paycheck.

lines.cap: The holidays? Start in January, and $600 over 24 paychecks is $25 each.
lines.say: The holidays? Start in January, and six hundred dollars over twenty-four paychecks is twenty-five dollars each.

scene.sub: Someday funds: fill to a target

lines.cap: Someday funds don't have a date. Car repairs, medical bills. Give each a target, like $500 and $300.
lines.say: Someday funds don't have a date. Car repairs, medical bills. Give each one a target, like five hundred and three hundred.
Fill them a little each paycheck. When you use one, refill it.
Step three. Automate it. Set a transfer to savings on the same day your paycheck lands, so you never have to decide.
One savings account is fine. Just track each fund's balance, or use a bank that lets you split savings into named buckets.

scene.head: SINKING FUNDS
items: Someday funds: fill to a target

lines.say: Recap.
List every cost that isn't monthly.
Deadline funds: divide the cost by the paychecks left.
Someday funds: fill to a target, and refill.
And automate it on payday.
